title: Transfusion: Autoregressive Text + Diffusion Image in One Transformer

questions.question: How does Transfusion train text and continuous image patches in one shared transformer?
options: Quantize image patches to VQ IDs and apply only next-token loss everywhere.
Use next-token loss on text and a diffusion or flow-matching loss on image patches.
Train separate text and image models, then average their final embeddings.
Use contrastive image-text loss for both modalities and no generation loss.
questions.explanation: Transfusion shares a transformer body but applies next-token cross-entropy to text tokens and diffusion/flow loss to continuous image patches. VQ-only next-token training is Chameleon’s discrete-image route and retains its tokenizer reconstruction ceiling.

questions.question: Which attention behavior does Transfusion use for a sequence containing text and one image block?
options: Text and image tokens use separate transformers with no cross-attention.
Text is causal; image patches attend bidirectionally within their image block.
All tokens attend bidirectionally across text and image regardless of order.
Text is bidirectional; image patches attend only to earlier patches.
questions.explanation: Causal masking on text prevents a token from seeing future text during teacher forcing. Patches within the same image block can attend bidirectionally because they form one snapshot; making all text bidirectional would leak future targets.

questions.question: A patch has clean value x0=2, sampled noise epsilon=6, and flow time t=0.25. Using xt=(1-t)x0+t*epsilon, what noisy value and target velocity result?
options: xt=4 and velocity=4.
xt=3 and velocity=-4.
xt=3 and velocity=4.
xt=2 and velocity=4.
questions.explanation: The noisy patch is xt=(1−0.25)×2+0.25×6=1.5+1.5=3, and the target velocity is ε−x0=6−2=4. Because noise exceeds the clean value, velocity is positive. The negative option reverses subtraction; xt=2 skips interpolation. For this linear path, velocity is epsilon minus clean, independent of t.

questions.question: What is the defining MMDiT change compared with Transfusion's fully shared transformer blocks?
options: A VQ codebook that replaces all continuous image patches.
One shared QKV projection but no image-to-text attention.
Separate modality-specific QKV and MLP weights with joint cross-modality attention.
Separate text and image models with no shared attention or hidden state.
questions.explanation: MMDiT gives text and image separate QKV/MLP weights while allowing joint cross-modality attention. This preserves interactions between modalities while letting each use different transformations; fully separate models have no shared attention stream.

questions.question: Assume 50 text tokens are generated autoregressively, then 256 image patches are denoised together for 20 steps. How many model forward passes are needed, excluding any guidance branch?
options: 20 passes total, because text generation shares the diffusion schedule.
306 passes: one text pass and one image pass per token.
50 passes total, because all image patches use a single denoising step.
70 passes: 50 text-token steps plus 20 image-denoising steps.
questions.explanation: Text generation takes 50 autoregressive forward passes, one per token; image denoising processes the 256 patches together each step, for 20 passes. Under the stated no-guidance assumption, total is 50+20=70.

questions.question: A team needs high-fidelity continuous image generation and can manage two loss heads. Which design tradeoff supports choosing Transfusion over Chameleon?
options: Discrete image IDs avoid any image-generation loop and guarantee higher fidelity.
A shared text vocabulary makes all image reconstruction losses unnecessary.
Continuous patches avoid a VQ quantization ceiling while text and images share one transformer.
Separate diffusion weights remove the need to train a shared backbone.
questions.explanation: Transfusion keeps image patches continuous, avoiding the VQ quantization ceiling, while one transformer also predicts text with NTP. It requires balancing two losses; Chameleon’s discrete-token route is simpler but may lose image detail.
